items.title: The Devil’s Hidden Strategy: Allen Parr Reveals How Christians Become Trapped
items.author: Billy Hallowell
items.summary: Encouraging.
items.content:
📖 News | Faithwire

Author and YouTuber Allen Parr is on a mission to help people think through the spiritual barriers that could be holding them back from a fruitful life.

Parr’s new book, “Breaking Through: How Ordinary Believers Experience Extraordinary Freedom,” is all about finding freedom. He relies on his own experiences to help readers explore this essential topic.

“When I look at my life, there’s a lot of challenges … I refer to them as soul chains, but really, that’s probably a synonym for strongholds, things that hold Christians back from walking in their full potential,” he said. “As Christians, we know we’re saved, we know that we are forgiven, we know we’re on our way to Heaven, and that’s great.”

Parr said the book’s premise is Jesus died to forgive human beings for their sins, but also to offer freedom so people can live a “life of abundance.”

“I wanted to write a book to help Christians understand how they can experience the freedom and the victorious life that Jesus promised us,” he said.

Parr also spoke about why some churches might not openly speak about matters pertaining to mental health or even spiritual warfare.

“Maybe one of the reasons why a lot of churches don’t want to deal with it is that they don’t really know how to go about addressing a lot of these things,” he said. “Because, as church leaders, we’re trained in the areas of apologetics. We’re trained in the area of theology and hermeneutics and all of that. But a lot of times, we’re not trained to understand how to deal with someone who’s dealing with serious mental health issues. So oftentimes, churches may not be equipped … to know how to handle it.”

He also spoke to another dynamic: the human penchant for picking extreme “either, or” positions on demons and the supernatural.

“We err on two extremes,” Parr said. “One extreme is, ‘Hey, you know, every single thing is a demon. Everything is a demon. Everything needs to be cast out. If you’re having a bad day, that’s the demon of depression that’s attacking you,'” he said. “No, it’s just life. We have difficult days.”

The author said the notion “everything is a demon” can heighten spiritual warfare and lead some people to exaggerate or sensationalize what they or others face. That said, he pointed to the other side of the paradigm.

“The other side is the other extreme, and that’s the fact that, ‘Hey, we’re not in a spiritual war. There is no such thing as demons and supernatural … and you just need to work everything out by yourself.”

Parr encouraged Christians to find common ground in the middle of these extremes, and pointed to the words of Ephesians 6 to make his point — a chapter in the Bible that discusses the wrestling humans face against spiritual powers.

He spoke about his own struggles and the “soul chains” so many people struggle with, including lust, among other issues. He believes these soul chains are sometimes formed as a result of emotional wounds.

“I struggled with toxic relationships, having grown up in a home where there was a lot of divorce,” Parr said. “My mom and dad got divorced multiple times over, and that created a fear in me to get into a committed relationship and a committed marriage.”

He said the devil often seizes upon these soul wounds to open up emotional pain. Parr said divorce created a chain of fear over getting married. He also had father wounds as his dad was around in his life but not living in his home.

“I talk about the soul chain of perfectionism, and I struggled with that,” he continued. “Lots of different things, a poverty mentality because we grew up without much money, and so all of these things are things that we don’t even realize a lot of times until we’re in our later stages of life.”

A lot of these issues are built on deception and will hold people back, he said.

“Every soul chain is established on some sort of lie that the enemy would want you to believe instead of the truth,” Parr said.

He believes it’s essential to pinpoint the “chains” holding people back so that they can be dealt with. Part of that process is having people in life who individuals are close with; these people can then raise issues they observe.

“So the question is, whenever people bring certain things up to you, like, ‘Hey, you’re dealing with perfectionism,’ or ‘Hey, I see this issue of anger in your life, or unforgiveness, or shame, low self-esteem,’ I mean, there’s a ton of them that I talk about in the book,” Parr said. “The question is, do you receive that, or are you resistant to that? Oftentimes, if we’re resistant, that’s a sign that maybe this thing has a chain and a hold on us that we’re not realizing.”

After identifying these ties, he said, “Breaking Through: How Ordinary Believers Experience Extraordinary Freedom,” offers an opportunity to explore a biblical roadmap to help walk toward freedom.

items.title: ‘They’re Demonic’: Astronaut Who Walked on the Moon on Shocking Truth About Aliens
items.author: Billy Hallowell
items.summary: "That's ... what God showed me."
items.content:
📖 News | Faithwire

Former astronaut Charlie Duke is known for being the youngest man to walk on the moon. But Duke, 91, is also a strong Christian who has a fascinating perspective on aliens and UFOs, subjects that have received a plethora of attention of late.

The astronaut, who was the spacecraft communicator for the Apollo 11 Moon landing in 1969 and spent 265 hours in space during that time, told CBN News he once wasn’t so sure about his beliefs on the true nature of aliens and UFOs.

“For a long time [years ago] I was praying about UFOs, and asked for a sign,” Duke said. “I felt like UFOs were demonic … but I was saying that at rotary clubs and stuff like that, and people were laughing me off the stage.”

So, he asked the Lord to help him come to a definitive conclusion that would settle the matter once and for all.

“I said, ‘God, if I’m really right about this, then give me a sign tomorrow morning that a very good friend of mine at breakfast will start talking about UFOs,'” he said. “And this guy’s a businessman. He never talks about science stuff or … stuff like that. So the next morning at breakfast, we sat down, he said, ‘Charlie, come on over. I wanna start talking to you about UFOs.'”

Duke interpreted this as an answer to his prayer. The former astronaut then appealed to Scripture to make his case, looking at the Bible’s description of Satan to further conclude his position.

“The Lord says what we’re seeing is real, but the devil can appear as an angel of light, the Bible says,” he said. “And so what I believe … is the UFOs are trying to turn us away from the truth and run after these alien beings, which are really not beings at all. They’re demonic.”

Ultimately, Duke said he’s unconcerned with those who might laugh at him or mock his perspective on the matter.

“You can laugh at me if you want to, but that’s … what God showed me, and I’m sticking to it,” he said.

Duke said he never personally viewed anything on his flight to the moon that would be considered alien or UFO-like. Watch the interview above for more.

items.title: Forrest Frank Announces ‘The Jesus Generation’ Tour Documentary, Coming to Theaters Next Year
items.author: RELEVANT Staff
items.summary: Forrest Frank has released the first trailer for The Jesus Generation, a documentary about his record-setting Jesus Generation Tour. Lionsgate will distribute the film, which includes appearances by Rick Rubin, Philip Anthony Mitchell and Sadie Robertson, among others. Forrest posted the teaser to Y
items.content:
📖 Culture | Relevant Magazine

Forrest Frank has released the first trailer for The Jesus Generation, a documentary about his record-setting Jesus Generation Tour. Lionsgate will distribute the film, which includes appearances by Rick Rubin, Philip Anthony Mitchell and Sadie Robertson, among others. Forrest posted the teaser to YouTube and Instagram, with a sign-up page for updates at forrestfrank.com.

A director and release date haven’t been announced yet.

The Jesus Generation Tour ran 29 cities from June 1 at the BOK Center in Tulsa, Oklahoma, to a sold-out finale at Globe Life Field in Arlington, Texas, where more than 35,000 people came. More than 519,000 people attended in two months, which makes it the biggest Christian music tour in history.

It also registered outside Christian music. One count named it the biggest arena tour overall.

Pollstar ranked the tour No. 5 on its LIVE75 chart in late June, behind Bad Bunny, BTS, Luke Combs and Iron Maiden, who were all playing stadiums. Pollstar said it was the highest chart position of any artist booked primarily in arenas. Early reported shows averaged about 18,000 tickets a night.

Hersheypark Stadium in Pennsylvania drew 27,365 people on June 15, and GEODIS Park in Nashville drew 23,667 four days later. Tori Kelly, Cory Asbury and The Figs supported the tour.

Demand was there before the first show. Pollstar reported in December that the tour had already passed 470,000 tickets sold. The growth is steep. His first headline run, the 2024 Child of God Tour, drew 48,246 people over 17 shows. The following year, the Child of God Tour Part 2 drew 214,626 fans to 26 shows. This year’s tour more than doubled that attendance.

The music behind it has been on a similar run. Child of God II debuted at No. 12 on the Billboard 200 and logged the most weeks at No. 1 on Billboard’s Top Christian Albums chart. “Your Way’s Better” was the No. 1 Hot Christian Song of 2025 and broke into the Hot 100. Forrest has also placed 70 songs on the Hot Christian Songs chart, the most of any artist.

items.title: A Tragedy in Education
items.author: Henry T. Edmondson III
items.summary:
Henry T. Edmondson III

Hannah-Jones and her husband sacrificed their daughter’s well-being in the interest of their muddled “values,” which look suspiciously like a political agenda.
items.content:
📖 Catholic Teaching | Word on Fire

Henry T. Edmondson III

Nikole Hannah-Jones offered her daughter to the Goddess of Public Education. The goddess failed her.

Hannah-Jones, as you may know, is the New York Times writer and progenitor of the infamous 1619 Project, a distortion of American history arguing that the driving force of the founding of America was the motivation to preserve slavery. 

Never mind that eminent American historians from both the right and the left have condemned the project: Hannah-Jones has been awarded a Pulitzer Prize, her initial essay in the New York Times Magazine is now a book, and there is now a high school curriculum based on the 1619 propaganda in between 4,500–5,000 schools. The 1619 project is part of the “Hate America” movement.

And propaganda it is, as Hannah-Jones has admitted that her reason for the project was political—that is, she was out to promote a political agenda, academic integrity be damned. In so doing, she is following a trend in the academic discipline of history, contending that the subject should be taught to bring about social and political change. Historical accuracy takes a back seat. 

Several years ago, Lucas Morel of Washington and Lee University elaborated on the impact of the 1619 Project:

Hannah-Jones is now collaborating with Oprah Winfrey and Lionsgate on film and television projects and has contracted with One World, a division of Penguin Random House, to publish an amplified book version of all the magazine essays plus books of essays, fiction, and poetry on the project theme. Random House Children’s Books will also produce 1619 Project books for young readers, and Random House’s Ten Speed Imprint will produce a graphic novel.

Betrayal

More recently, Hannah-Jones was back in The New York Times on September 20 with an essay confessing that she has betrayed her daughter by deliberately sending her to a deficient public school. Her daughter Najya, now sixteen, resents her parents’ choice. The essay is a chronicle of a failed education deliberately orchestrated by her parents.

Before going further, let me be clear: This essay is not an attack on public schools. Far from it. We all have a vested interest in the success of public education and should support it in any way we can, even if some of us have chosen an alternative of our own. The American founders—such as Thomas Jefferson, George Washington, and Benjamin Rush—argued emphatically that the success of the American project rests on properly educated citizens. 

This essay, however, is an observation of how misguided—if not immoral—efforts to improve public schools may be, and it tells us something about why public schools are not improving when they could be.

She begins,

A decade ago, I made a decision about my daughter’s education that I hoped would challenge New York City’s separate and unequal school system. Now 16, she thinks I made the wrong choice.

The essay continues as her daughter Najya realizes what her mother and father had done. She asks, 

“Did you know my school was bad like this when you decided to put me here?” she asked. . . . By dismissal time, Najya’s shock had turned to boiling, and the seatbelt had barely clicked before she was confronting me.

Najya, an ambitious student now thinking about her future, continues with her indictment of her parents, 

“We looked up our school! We saw the test scores. We saw the ratings.” She ticked off the school’s below-state average reading and math scores, and that it ranked poorly on a popular school-rating website. 

Hannah-Jones and her husband knew exactly what they had done. She writes, 

When Najya was entering pre-K, my husband, Faraji, and I decided to send her to the type of school that wealthier families with choices uniformly avoid—one that is low-income and mostly Black. Our decision had been informed by values shaped by my years of reporting on the enduring and too often seemingly hopeless battle for school integration.

Hannah-Jones never explains her “values” throughout the essay, but whatever they are, they justified sending her daughter, beginning in kindergarten, to the worst school available rather than the best.
Word on Fire’s Liturgy of the Hours is Here!
Order Your Set Today

Hannah-Jones and her husband, by contrast, had attended much better schools and had “flourished academically.” Not including Faraji’s net worth, Nikole Hannah-Jones is estimated to have a net worth of at least $3 million. They could have sent Najya most anywhere. So why send her to an inferior school? The answer is shocking:

So, like the generations of Black parents who came before us, Faraji and I felt an obligation to make educational decisions based on the collective good and not just our individual advantage. . . . Faraji and I decided that our role in this struggle meant upending the status quo and sending our child not to a wealthy white school but to a poor Black one.

She explains, “We thought by sending Najya to a mostly low-income and Black school, we could help improve it for all the children there.” She admits, “But my child just shook her head, her face a mask of disbelief, and something else: betrayal.”

Najya was asking what I’d accomplished by not choosing the “best” school for her. And the honest answer is, I don’t know. When it comes to the choices my husband and I have made about public education, these days I feel that I failed both my values and my child. 

More accurately, Hannah-Jones put her “values”—whatever that ambiguous word means—before the welfare of her child. Such “values” seem quite destructive and morally confused. This drove her to prefer “the group” over an individual child—their only child. Although she would not admit it, and probably doesn’t even understand it, such a disordered collectivism is a relic of Marxism, which has failed both the individual and the group.

Sixteen-year-old Najya proved wiser and in possession of more common sense than her parents.

I explained our decision over and over, but my answers never satisfied her. “But what did it do?” she’d ask. “Putting me in this school didn’t change anything. . . . It makes no sense.”

Faux Nobility

Hannah-Jones is a martyr for some and assumes a noble pose in her essay—but it is unwarranted. When making their decision to send Najya to a culturally and academically poor school, Hannah-Jones writes that her family joined the ranks of the “Little Rock Nine,” the black students who entered Little Rock Central High School in 1957 after the unanimous landmark Supreme Court case Brown v. Board of Education (1954). In doing so, they were the first crack in the dam of school segregation. It was a heart-wrenching, violent experience, but they planted themselves squarely in the heritage of the Civil Rights Movement in the United States. As time has passed, they have justly received numerous prestigious awards, including the Congressional Gold Medal.

But there are two problems with this comparison. One, these students were of high school age, and they knew what they were doing. Najya did not find out until it was much too late that her parents had acted contrary to her best interests. She knew nothing of her parents’ awful decision until she discovered it herself.

Secondly, the Little Rock Nine’s bravery changed the world, but as Hannah-Jones confesses, she and her husband accomplished nothing. Although she calls her essay a “confession,” it is more of an abdication of guilt and an indictment of a system that tolerates schools such as the one to which she and her husband sentenced their daughter. Yet if condemnation of public education in the US were going to make a difference, we’d have the best public schools on the planet. But we don’t.

Hannah-Jones describes her choice to prioritize the “system” over her daughter as a “sacrifice,” but that implies that her daughter made the choice when she did not. Rather, Hannah-Jones and her husband sacrificed their daughter’s well-being in the interest of their muddled “values,” which look suspiciously like a political agenda.

In another lapse of intellectual integrity, Hannah-Jones creates a straw man and then attacks it when she claims that, rather than work for school improvement, “we have instead chosen to succumb to a collective apathy in the face of a system so devastatingly unequal that it puts at odds trying to be a good person with trying to be a good parent.” But who are the “we” who have “succumbed to a collective apathy”? She doesn’t say. I personally don’t know anyone who is apathetic about “a devastatingly unequal” education, but maybe I run with the wrong crowd.

Moreover, she claims the problem with public schools is racism and the refusal of “those who hold the most power to change.” She further—probably unwittingly—invokes Aristotle’s distinction between a good person and a good citizen. In Book III of Politics, Aristotle said that a good citizen must sometimes act contrary to the regime in which they live if that regime is flawed. In that sense, they may not be a “good,” obedient citizen. In this case, however, Hannah-Jones creates a dilemma between a good person and a good parent. In other words, the “system” has prevented her from being both a good person and a good parent. There’s no nice way to put it: this is nonsense. 
Magnificent Humanity
Get Pope Leo’s Encyclical

Her closing paragraph reveals she has still failed to understand—or admit—that she outrageously failed her daughter because, in Hannah-Jones’s own words, she did not “rescue” her daughter from a poor education. At best, she claims, if there is guilt, it is collective guilt.

But for all of our justifications, including mine, an undeniable verity remains. As long as we continue to rescue our own children from the failing schools where we allow other people’s children to languish simply because those children have been born Black and poor in a nation of racism and riches, there is no absolution here. Not for me. Not for you. Not for any of us. 

The best that can be said for that closing declaration is that it is confused and confusing. 

Only One Chance at Fourth Grade

In writing this essay, replete with pictures of her daughter from kindergarten through high school, Hannah-Jones tempts the reader to ask: Is she exploiting her child—again? We all now know exactly what Najya looks like from kindergarten into high school. The whole world also knows that she is poorly educated. 

If they had really wanted to change the system and do the best for their daughter, what else could her parents have done? Let’s see: They could have sent Najya to the best school available, and since they were a family of means, they could have funded the same opportunity for several other children. Then, over time, they might have donated the seed money for a more general scholarship program. Indeed, several such programs were established in honor of the Little Rock Nine. Or they might have put their energy and money behind a public charter school or a public magnet school. Or they might have located a struggling public school and volunteered there, even occasionally serving as guest teachers. Her husband is an IT professional, and she is a newspaper writer—just don’t let her teach American history. 

The problem, however, is that for Democrats, scholarship programs are anathema because not everyone receives scholarships. This is “equality” run amuck. Some Democratic politicians and the leftist Teacher Unions (e.g., the NEA and the AFT) have gone so far as to try and destroy the massively popular Washington, DC, Opportunity Scholarship Program. Najya has consistently proven smarter than her parents. She asked,

“So you had money to send me to one of the best schools, and you chose not to?” she said, hurling her words. “Because other kids are disadvantaged, you didn’t want to put me in a great school?”

It is not unusual for some to criticize parents when they choose a private school, a religious school, or a homeschool over a public school. As we have learned, however, many of these critics, if they have the means, will themselves send their offspring to private schools. We have seen it time and again. We can’t blame them: It would be irresponsible to do anything else, if there is no public school within reach. They realize that their child has only one opportunity for each grade level. 

At the same time, however, they oppose such opportunities for families without the means to do the same. 

The hypocrisy is insufferable.

items.title: Friday, October 23, 2026
items.author: Bishop Robert Barron
items.summary:
Bishop Robert Barron

Friends, in today’s Gospel, Jesus criticizes the crowd by saying that they could interpret the earth and the clouds but do not know how to interpret the present time.
items.content:
📖 Catholic Teaching | Word on Fire

Bishop Robert Barron

Daily Reading


First Reading
Ephesians 4:1-6

I therefore, the prisoner in the Lord, beg you to lead a life worthy of the calling to which you have been called, with all humility and gentleness, with patience, bearing with one another in love, making every effort to maintain the unity of the Spirit in the bond of peace. There is one body and one Spirit, just as you were called to the one hope of your calling, one Lord, one faith, one baptism, one God and Father of all, who is above all and through all and in all.

Psalm
Psalm 24:1-2, 3-4ab, 5-6

The earth is the Lord’s and all that is in it,
    the world, and those who live in it;
for he has founded it on the seas,
    and established it on the rivers.
Who shall ascend the hill of the Lord?
    And who shall stand in his holy place?
Those who have clean hands and pure hearts,
    who do not lift up their souls to what is false,
    and do not swear deceitfully.
They will receive blessing from the Lord,
    and vindication from the God of their salvation.
Such is the company of those who seek him,
    who seek the face of the God of Jacob. Selah

Gospel Reading
Luke 12:54-59

 He also said to the crowds, “When you see a cloud rising in the west, you immediately say, ‘It is going to rain’; and so it happens. And when you see the south wind blowing, you say, ‘There will be scorching heat’; and it happens. You hypocrites! You know how to interpret the appearance of earth and sky, but why do you not know how to interpret the present time?

“And why do you not judge for yourselves what is right? Thus, when you go with your accuser before a magistrate, on the way make an effort to settle the case, or you may be dragged before the judge, and the judge hand you over to the officer, and the officer throw you in prison. I tell you, you will never get out until you have paid the very last penny.”

Reflection

Friends, in today’s Gospel, Jesus criticizes the crowd by saying that they could interpret the earth and the clouds but do not know how to interpret the present time.

So, how do we know what’s going on in the world? How do we read the signs of the times? We could do so politically, sociologically, culturally, or economically. All these ways are valuable lenses for viewing the world. But note the important difference in the Bible.

What was peculiar about ancient Israel was their reading the world through theological lenses. When they wanted to read the signs of the times, they wondered what God was doing and why. The deepest and truest reading is the theological one that seeks after the divine causality and purpose that works under and through all the other lenses.

The modern period has become largely conditioned by a deist view of God, whereby God is construed as a distant object only vaguely related to the world. On this reading, God does not actively involve himself in the affairs of economics, politics, or culture. Ah! But that’s not the biblical reading. For the biblical authors, God acts in and through all the ordinary events and dynamics of the world.
